metadata.title: Kikiria
metadata.description: A game to look, ask and check what you find online.

home.mascotAlt: Roqui, a little detective rooster holding a magnifying glass.
home.title: Can you figure out which one was made with AI?
dialogue: Hi! I’m Roqui, the detective rooster.
Have you ever seen a photo and wondered if it was real?
Computers can now invent photos that look real.
I’ll teach you how to spot them!

briefing: Mission 1! Find the image made with AI.
You will see two images: one is a photo and the other was made by a computer.
Tap the one you think the computer made.
Getting it wrong is fine: that is how we learn.

r1.observation: Check whether something repeats in exactly the same way.
r1.remember: It is a clue, not proof.

r2.question: Who posted this picture, and what for?

r3.verification: Find where it came from before believing it.
r3.remember: Sometimes looking is not enough to know.

r1.observation: Look at the paws and the ears: does anything look odd?
r1.remember: One odd detail does not always mean AI.

r2.question: Who is sharing this animal picture, and why?
r2.remember: The picture alone does not tell the whole story.

r3.verification: Ask a grown-up where the image came from.
r3.remember: Being unsure is a valid answer too.

r1.observation: Quick: check the background, not only the animal.
r1.remember: Going fast is not the same as not looking.

r2.question: Why would someone want to post this?
r2.remember: Many pictures are made to be shared.

r3.verification: If you run out of time, say you do not know.
r3.remember: Saying "I don't know" beats making it up.

r1.observation: Look at the hands and the feet: they are the hardest to fake.
r1.remember: A clue tells you to keep looking, not to decide.

r2.question: Who gained something by posting this image?
r2.remember: There is always someone behind an image.

r3.verification: Check whether a known outlet published it.
r3.remember: If nobody confirms it, we still do not know.

r1.observation: With no second picture, look for blurry edges and things that repeat.
r1.remember: This time it is your call: there is nothing to compare.

r2.question: Does it look like a photo anyone could have taken?
r2.remember: Ordinary and dull is often real.

r3.verification: If you are unsure, say so and find where it came from.
r3.remember: Being unsure is not failing: it is what a detective does.

r1.observation: Check the crowd and the background, not only the main figure.
r1.remember: AI usually slips where nobody is looking.

r2.question: Why would this be shown to you?
r2.remember: An image always comes from someone with a purpose.

r3.verification: Before sharing it, find who published it first.
r3.remember: Sharing without checking is part of the problem too.

r1.verification: A photo this ordinary could be anyone's. You have to find where it came from.
r1.remember: Saying "you cannot tell" is a detective's answer, not giving up.

r2.question: Who was there, and what did they take this photo for?
r2.remember: When you can tell, say so. Doubting everything is no use either.

r3.verification: A face can be invented or real. Only the source settles it.
r3.remember: Looking gives you clues. The source gives you the answer.

r1.observation: Compare frame with frame: count the fingers in each one.
r1.remember: Something that changes for no reason between frames is a clue.

r2.observation: Read the sign in all three frames: does it say the same thing every time?
r2.remember: Text inside a video is usually the first thing to slip.

r3.verification: If a video looks odd, find where it came from before believing it.
r3.remember: A video can look perfect and its origin still be unknown.

r1.observation: With no second video beside it, check the movement is even between frames.
r1.remember: Odd movement is a clue, not proof.

r2.question: What might this video have been made for?
r2.remember: A short video is made to be shared quickly.

r3.verification: Sometimes the frames are not enough: find the whole video and its source.
r3.remember: \"You cannot tell\" is still a detective's answer.

r1.observation: Check whether the background and the objects fit together.
r1.remember: Fitting together does not prove where it came from.

r2.question: What would a picture like this be posted for?
r2.remember: Behind every post there is an intention.

r3.verification: Before believing it, find who published it first.
r3.remember: The source counts for more than the detail.

r1.observation: Look at the photo, not at the caption. Anyone can write a caption.
r1.remember: Text on top says nothing about where the image came from.

r2.question: Why would they want you to share this?
r2.remember: Something funny can also be made to mislead.

r3.verification: Find the photo without the caption before forwarding it.
r3.remember: Forwarding without checking is part of the problem.

r1.verification: A meme usually comes from another meme. Who took the first photo is almost never known.
r1.remember: \"You cannot tell\" is often the honest answer.

r2.question: Who gained something from this meme being shared?
r2.remember: A meme travels because somebody wanted it to.

r3.verification: The words on top can completely change what the photo seems to show.
r3.remember: Separate the picture from the text: they are two different things.

round1.observation: Some letters do not form words.
round1.remember: It is a clue, not proof.

round2.question: Who published this image, and why?
round2.remember: Appearance does not tell the whole story.

round3.verification: Find the source and review the context.
round3.remember: We cannot always know just by looking.

teacher.title: Classroom guide
teacher.lead: This is how Kikiria works in a classroom. No internet needed, and no phones for the students.
teacher.sessionLead: The timings are a guide: if the discussion gets good, let it run.

welcome.title: Ask before you show
welcome.detail: Have you seen pictures online that looked real and were not? Let them tell you.

play.title: Play the first island
play.detail: Hand the phone to someone and let the rest argue out loud before they tap.

versus.title: Versus in turns
versus.detail: Two volunteers pass the phone. The others may give clues, never the answer.

talk.title: Talk it over
talk.detail: Use the prompts below. Getting it right matters less than explaining why.

close.title: Close with a rule
close.detail: Each child names one thing they will check before believing or sharing something.

teacher.promptsLead: They work even if the class got everything wrong. Doubt is the point.

prompts.one: What was the first thing that made you doubt that image?
prompts.two: Who do you think posted that photo, and what for?
prompts.three: Have you ever shared something without checking? What happened?
prompts.four: When is it fine to say "I do not know if this is real"?

teacher.onlineDescription: A code for your students to join, and a view of where the group struggles. It needs a server, and does not exist yet.
teacher.certificateDescription: Recognition for completing the training. It will arrive once the online classroom works.
teacher.privacyNote: The app never asks for a child's real name, age or school. In this version there are no accounts and nothing is uploaded to any server.
teacher.wayCardsDetail: You are the only one with a device. Each student holds up a sheet and you scan the answers with the camera.
teacher.wayPhonesDetail: If some students do have a phone, share the Kikiria address and each of them plays their own progress.
teacher.cardsHowLead: Start to finish. This is the part nobody guesses on their own.

create.title: You say how many students there are
create.detail: Kikiria makes a different sheet for each one, with their number and their code.

print.title: You print the sheets
print.detail: In black and white. One sheet per student, nothing to cut.

hand.title: You hand one to each student
hand.detail: The big number on the sheet is their id. No name is needed.

ask.title: You ask a question with two options
ask.detail: Read it aloud or show it on screen: option A and option B.

raise.title: They hold the sheet up, turned
raise.detail: For A, the A stays on top. For B, they turn the sheet upside down.

read.title: You scan with the camera
read.detail: Walk around the room and Kikiria notes who answered what, and who is missing.

briefing: Mission 1! This exercise has an authored answer.
A strange detail can be a clue, but it is not proof by itself.
Check who published an image, where it came from, and whether reliable sources confirm it.
AI-made content is not automatically false, and human-made content is not automatically trustworthy. Check the evidence and context.
education.visualClue: A visual detail may be a clue, but editing, compression, or ordinary mistakes can cause odd details too.
education.sourceQuestion: Who published this, and is the original source available? Compare it with reliable sources.
education.evidenceCheck: Is the image in its original context, and is there enough evidence to decide?
education.remember: In this exercise the origin is known. Outside the game, a clue alone does not prove where content came from.

accessModes.presentationTitle: How you want to see it and hear it
accessModes.presentationLead: These options change how the game is presented without changing your answers or progress.
accessModes.switchesLead: Each option on its own, in case you only want one.
accessModes.ownPacePresetFor: For anyone who is easily distracted
accessModes.ownPacePresetDetail: You can listen to the prompt, and movement is reduced while you decide.
accessModes.clearReadingPresetFor: For anyone who finds reading harder
accessModes.clearReadingPresetDetail: You can listen to the prompt, and text gets larger and more spaced out.
accessModes.noPenalty: These options do not change the correct answer or your progress.
accessModes.readAloudDetail: A button reads the question, the options and the explanation at the end out loud.
accessModes.readAloudUnavailable: Reading aloud is not available on this browser or device in this language.
accessModes.clearReadingDetail: Slightly larger text, more spacing, and a more comfortable reading width.
accessModes.reducedMotionDetail: Reduces nonessential movement while you decide.
accessModes.largerTextDetail: Size only, in case that is all you need.
accessModes.whyTitle: Why doesn't any button say "ADHD mode"?
accessModes.whyBody: You don't need a diagnosis to use these options. We designed them with different ways of reading, focusing and processing information in mind. If an option helps you, you can use it.
accessModes.whyHonest: Kikiria does not diagnose or treat any condition. These options change how content is presented, and you can use them without a diagnosis.

footer.notice: No account is required. Your profile and progress stay on this device.
